Sanitised HTML, cross-shadow selection and Temporal snapshots

I wanted to test three newer browser APIs directly alongside a drawable 2D canvas: inserting untrusted markup with Element.setHTML(), reading a cross-shadow selection with getSelection().getComposedRanges(), and stamping captureElementImage() frames with Temporal.

1. Element.setHTML() into a drawable canvas

Edit the untrusted HTML below, toggle which safe tags the Sanitizer keeps, and press Sanitise and draw. The clean markup goes straight into a drawable child of a 2D canvas, a scan line sweeps across the new DOM, and the diff lists what setHTML() stripped and what stayed.

      3. Temporal timestamps on captured DOM snapshots

      Edit the note card inside the canvas or press Mark edit, then capture single frames or a 1-second burst of 4 frames. Each capture calls canvas.captureElementImage(), stamps the snapshot with Temporal.Now.instant() and Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO(), and draws the last 4 frames along the filmstrip while closing every evicted ElementImage.

      Open snapshots: 0 / 4. Evicted and closed: 0.

        1. The editable note card is a drawable child of the same 2D canvas that draws the filmstrip.
        2. Stamp each snapshot with Temporal.Now and call close() on evicted frames and on pagehide.
        3. Draw the frozen filmstrip frames first and the live note card last so clicks land on the live inputs.

        How it works

        Every canvas on this page uses a 2D context scaled to its backing device pixels via a ResizeObserver. Each ctx.drawElementImage() call passes explicit CSS width and height so elements stay at 1:1 size on high-density screens instead of scaling by devicePixelRatio twice.

        In the first experiment, Element.setHTML() parses and sanitises untrusted markup directly into the drawable <article> child. A separate inert DOMParser parse of the raw string computes the tag and attribute diff without running scripts or fetching images. For 700 ms after each sanitisation, requestAnimationFrame calls requestPaint() so the scan line sweeps across the newly painted DOM and then stops.

        In the second experiment, <shadow-sel-box> puts its drawable canvas inside an open shadow root. When selectionchange fires, the page compares getSelection().getRangeAt(0) with getSelection().getComposedRanges({ shadowRoots: [shadow] }). Because a StaticRange has no getClientRects() method and a single live Range can't span a shadow boundary, the script slices the composed range against the shadow root's text nodes to collect line rectangles and paints a ribbon behind the text before calling drawElementImage().

        In the third experiment, pressing Capture frame sets a pending flag and requests a paint so captureElementImage() runs right after the latest edit paints. The filmstrip holds at most 4 ElementImage objects; adding a fifth calls close() on the oldest snapshot, and pagehide closes every remaining snapshot. During paint, the filmstrip thumbnails draw first and the live note card draws last, because the last drawElementImage() call for an element determines its hit box.

        Findings

        • Not verified yet in headless Chromium 157 or on Chrome for Android: run the live checks on this page to verify Element.setHTML(), getSelection().getComposedRanges(), selection.direction and Temporal.Now alongside drawElementImage() and captureElementImage() in your browser.
        • StaticRange from getComposedRanges() doesn't expose getClientRects(), so painting a canvas highlight across a shadow boundary still requires projecting the composed endpoints onto live Range instances inside each tree.
        • Drawing captured ElementImage thumbnails before the live editable card on the same canvas keeps clicks and typing aligned with the live controls while avoiding a second canvas context.
        • Calling close() on every evicted ElementImage and on pagehide caps open snapshots at 4 during normal use and returns open count to 0 when cleared.
